items.label: f02-order-snapshots
items.front: Why does an order item copy the product name, SKU and unit price?
items.back: Later catalogue edits must not rewrite what the customer ordered. The product reference stays for inventory restoration; the snapshot preserves the original commercial description.

items.label: f03-archive-not-delete
items.front: An admin tries to delete a product that appears in past orders. What happens and why?
items.back: 409: deleteMany requires orderItems: none, because history and cancellation still reference the product. Archive it instead, which hides it from new purchases but keeps the row.

items.label: f01-three-identities
items.front: Customer identity, record version, retry identity: what does each answer at checkout?
items.back: Token subject: who is acting (never a submitted userId). Record version: which accepted state an editor started from (conditional writes). Checkout key: which logical create attempt, stored durably per customer, so a retry after an uncertain response returns the same order.

items.label: f04-payment-timeout
items.front: A payment provider call times out. Is it safe to charge again?
items.back: No: a timeout can mean rejection, no contact, or acceptance without a delivered response. Persist the payment intent first, use a stable provider idempotency key, record observed outcomes, and reconcile; webhooks need signature checks, dedup and an allowed-transition policy.

To make the checkout key look consistent wherever the admin UI displays it
PostgreSQL rejects upper-case UUID strings when they are inserted into a uuid column type
It keys the advisory lock and the receipt lookup, so two casings cannot pass separately

Read 1 stops callers locking orders they can't see, and read 2 sees the state after the lock
Prisma requires an ordinary read before any raw query inside a transaction
The second read is redundant and exists only so the audit row can record the order's status

The first succeeds and the second is waitlisted until the product is restocked by an admin

choices.text: A new order is placed, as the old one is already cancelled
It returns the order as CANCELLED and reserves nothing
A 409 conflict, as a cancelled order cannot be replayed
The cancelled order is reopened as PENDING and stock is reserved again

items.prompt: Why does a popular product's admin edit history disappear after a few dozen orders?

choices.text: Each checkout overwrites the product's previous audit row instead of adding one
Admin edits are not audited at all; only order reservations write audit events
Audit events older than 30 days are removed by a nightly retention job
The newest 30 events are returned, and each order adds RESERVE/RESTORE events

Prisma increments the version column automatically on any update to a model that has one
To invalidate the cached product page so the storefront shows the new stock level right away
To record how many times the product has been sold, which the admin dashboard reports as popularity

PostgreSQL only grants FOR UPDATE locks in primary-key order within a single transaction
So the cheapest product is reserved first and the expensive ones fail fast if stock runs out
All checkouts then lock products in one common order, which rules out circular waits and deadlock

A new order: it replaces the first and releases that order's stock
The existing order: it is marked replayed and nothing new is reserved
409: that checkout key has already been used once

choices.text: The frontend disables the Cancel button after one click, and that is the only guard there is
Stock restoration is idempotent, as it writes stock as an absolute value, not a delta
The second waits on the lock, then sees a new version or CANCELLED status and conflicts
The second cancellation restores stock, but a nightly job corrects the count
